title.narrative: CRS - Multisectoral Assistance in the Kasais

description.narrative: The intervention is multi-sectorial and aim to reach 99 villages with integrated development package. The packages largely aim at reducing food insecurity from an agricultural perspective but also addresses livelihoods, nutritional needs, gender issues and social cohesion aspects. The global objective is the revival of sustainable agriculture, essential to reduce poverty, to ensure food and nutritional security for the populations of 99 villages of Lupatapata (in the Mukumbi health zone) and to generate sustainable jobs and income. More specifically, three major priority areas have been identified: Communities are equipped to maintain social cohesion. (ii) Communities adopt improved nutritional practices and produce more food for consumption and sale. (iii) 99 villages prioritize gender inclusion at community and household level. The activities (i) will help the communities to establish or reactivate their Community Animation Cell, to develop a set of key village development plans and to connect the communities to the main government services and structures. These activities will provide the foundations for villages and their members to describe and implement a shared vision for their village and establish renewed and strengthened relationships with key local government stakeholders. Households adopt improved agricultural practices to increase production. The project will support smallholder farmers in each village to organize themselves into PO (producer organisation) using training on the CRS SMART Skills curriculum. SMART Skills teach farmers a range of skills to improve their livelihoods, including how to organize into groups, use natural resources sustainably, market produce profitably, manage finances, and save money and organize credit, all while identifying, testing and adopting innovations. SMART Skills enables farmers to make the most of their resources and to prepare for recurrent shocks and chronic stresses. The SMART curriculum is skills-based and organizes these topics under five key skills: (Group management/organization, Natural Resource Management, Finance, Marketing, Innovation). Communities promote gender inclusion in governance activities: CRS will seek greater female participation across SO1 activities by including the training of “Gender Champions” to act as community-level advocates for increased awareness of issues relating to gender equality. The 198 Gender Champions - a man and woman nominated by each of the 99 target villages’ CAC in consultation with the village chief - will participate in a three-day training in Mbuji Mayi on topics including SGBV prevention, the importance of joint decision making among couples, changing norms around child and forced marriage, among other topics identified during the gender analysis included in the baseline assessement.

Befolkningen som lever i Lupatatapa i provinsen Kasai Oriental lider av fattigdom och undernäring trots områdets rika naturtillgångar, bördiga mark och stora potential till självförsörjande jordbruk. Provinsen är rik på mineraler, främst diamanter, men paradoxalt nog lider befolkningen av kronisk fattigdom och det finns bristande kunskaper om jordbruk, boskap och fiske för att livnära sig. Provinsen kännetecknas även av dålig infrastruktur med obefintliga vägar, och ett ineffektivt transportsystem vilket gör det svårt för småskaliga jordbrukare att transportera sina råvaror. Catholics Relief Resources (CRS) bad Sida om ett bidrag på 55 696 948 SEK för aktuellt projekt under perioden 2021–2024. Interventionen är ett multisektoriellt biståndsprojekt som främst syftar till att återinföra hållbart jordbruk för att förbättra inkomsterna för samhällen i 99 byar på Lupatapatas territorium. Grödorna som omfattas är majs, soja, sötpotatis, moringa samt fjäderfäuppfödning. CRS kommer inte begränsa projektet till jordbruk, utan avser anta ett holistiskt tillvägagångssätt för att gynna till positiv utveckling, social integration och samhällsstyrning med betoning på att kvinnor inkluderas i styrelseformer samt i alla utvecklingsaktiviteter. En hållbar jordbruksproduktion och försörjning avser leda till ökad livsmedelssäkerhet i de 99 byar som projektet riktar sig till. CRS kommer att samarbeta med lokala icke-statliga organisationer för att öka de tekniska kunskaperna i området, och utveckla byarnas samarbete vad gäller styrning samt koppla samman de olika grupperna av producenter. De förväntade resultaten är: - Gemenskaperna ska bli utrustade för att upprätthålla social sammanhållning. - Styrelsestrukturer på gemenskapsnivå ska stärkas, bli aktiva och kopplade till statliga tjänster. - Hushållen ska använda förbättrade näringsmetoder. Samhällen ska producera mer mat för konsumtion och försäljning. - Gemenskaper ska mobilisera resurser för att få tillgång till näringsrik mat. - De berörda 99 byarna ska prioritera genderfrågor på samhälls- och hushållsnivå. Den totala budgeten för insatsen uppgår till maximalt 57 716 948 SEK för genomförandet av Tudikolela-projektet under perioden 2021–2024.

The population of Lupatatapa in the province of Kasai Oriental is very poor and suffers from malnutrition despite the area's rich natural resources, fertile land and great potential for self-sufficient agriculture. The province is rich in minerals, mainly diamonds, however this is not benefiting the local population who suffers from chronic poverty. There is also lack of knowledge of agriculture, livestock and fishing to sustain themselves. The province is characterized by poor infrastructure with non-existent roads, and an inefficient transport system which makes it difficult for small-scale farmers to transport their commodities. Catholics Relief Resources (CRS) asked Sida for a grant of SEK 55 696 948 for the current project during the period 2021-2024. The intervention is a multi-sectoral aid project that primarily aims to reintroduce sustainable agriculture to improve the income of communities in 99 villages in the territory of Lupatapata. The crops covered are maize, soya, sweet potato, moringa and poultry farming. CRS will not limit the project to agriculture but intends to adopt a holistic approach to favour positive development, social inclusion and governance with emphasis on the inclusion of women in governance and in all development activities. Sustainable agricultural production and livelihoods will lead to increased food security in the 99 villages targeted by the project. CRS will work with local non-governmental organisations to increase technical knowledge in the area, develop village cooperation in governance and connect the different groups of producers. The expected results are: - Communities will be equipped to maintain social cohesion. - Community-level governance structures will be strengthened, active and linked to government services. - Households will adopt improved nutritional practices. Communities will produce more food for consumption and sale. - Communities will mobilise resources to access nutritious food. - The 99 villages concerned will prioritise gender inclusion at community and household level. The Swedish Embassy will contribute with up to 57 716 948 SEK for the implementation of the the Tudikolela project during the period 2021-2024.

The Tudikolela project (We Are Capable in English), implemented from 2021 to 2024 by Catholic Relief Services (CRS) in consortium with local organizations, Caritas Développement Mbujimayi, and REFED, was deployed in the Lupatapata territory (KasaiOriental province). This multisectoral initiative reached more than 93,000 direct and indirect beneficiaries, representing 17,615 households across 99 villages. The originality of this intervention lies in its ability to address food insecurity not as a simple agricultural production issue, but as a systemic challenge where social cohesion, village economies, and gender equality are interconnected to build sustainable resilience. The project was highly praised by Sweden, both by the local population and provincial authorities, for the results it generated and the positive change it brought to the area. Key results achieved: 99 villages in the Mukumbi health zone are implementing community development initiatives and are equipped to maintain social cohesion. Thanks to invaluable support from Sweden, a transformative path has emerged in the heart of these 99 villages. All 99 targeted villages benefited from comprehensive support, structured around conflict management training and social cohesion workshops. Peace clubs were established to restore dialogue, while the participatory development of multisectoral Local Development Plans (LDPs) empowered residents to plan their future. On the ground, the pride of the village chiefs was palpable as they presented these plans, developed in close collaboration with the Regional Health Council (CRS). This inclusive approach, commended by Sweden, places the population at the center of identifying its own needs. Such commitment from traditional leaders ensures strong local ownership, an essential guarantee of the sustainability of these initiatives. The most significant impact of this dynamic lie in the resolution of a long standing conflict. The tensions that had existed between the Bakua Mpuka 2 and Bajila Kasanga 2 groups (Eastern Kasai) and those of Bena Dilungi and Bakua Mfika (Central Kasai) were eased thanks to peace clubs. Successive dialogues facilitated by the CRS (Center for Peace and Reconciliation) mobilized provincial authorities, allowing for a shared understanding of the issues and the development of a consensus. On the ground, progress is tangible: an end to harassment related to customary land rights, arbitration by the authorities for a final decision, and a resumption of fluid communication between the chiefs. The culmination of this process took place at Lake Munkamba, where the chiefs of the opposing groups warmly shook hands at the conclusion of the discussions, thus sealing a strong signal of lasting peace. Faced with the lack of formal banking institutions, a common situation in rural areas, the Tudikolela project structured farmers into solidarity based self-savings groups, known as SILC groups. Each week, members purchase shares, which then feed into a self-managed internal credit fund. To strengthen this model, permaculture gardens were integrated around the farms, while the producers unexpectedly initiated the reforestation of over 240,000 fast-growing seedlings. This initiative, praised by the Swedish Embassy, retains water in the soil and helps farmers adapt to the effects of climate change, such as extreme heat and disrupted seasons. Thanks to this dynamic, the 299 savings communities have mobilized over USD 140,000 in credit, promoting crucial financial inclusion. The beneficiaries used these funds to launch small income-generating activities, such as small pharmacies or the sale of necessities, corn, charcoal, and seeds. During embassy field visits, the men and women involved in the project demonstrated their ability to finance their children's education and provide for their families. To protect these gains from financial tensions, 792 members of the management committees were trained in resolving financial conflicts, thus securing the funds and preventing household depletion through an emergency social fund. To crown these efforts, community celebrations were organized under the leadership of Community Animation Cells. Highly praised by the population, village chiefs, and Sweden, these celebrations included open mic sessions, music, and plays raising awareness about peace, social cohesion, and the fight against sexual and gender-based violence, thereby strengthening community unity. Ninetynine villages in the Mukumbi health zone are taking steps to improve their food and nutritional security. Eastern Kasai is experiencing a multidimensional crisis where food insecurity and chronic malnutrition are exacerbated by fragile local governance and recurring land disputes over natural resources. Although small-scale agriculture and mining dictate the region's economic rhythm, their structural weaknesses fail to stem mass unemployment, perpetuating widespread poverty. At the heart of this system, women carry out a large share of agricultural activities but remain marginalized from decision-making and control over the financial benefits of their own labor. Faced with these challenges, Sweden's decision to collaborate in a consortium with local actors proves particularly relevant for ensuring the sustainability of interventions. Catholic Relief Services' (CRS) approach aligns perfectly with the Swedish strategy by operating at the intersection of humanitarian emergency response, long-term development, and peacebuilding, while prioritizing the strengthening of market systems. This strategic synergy has enabled CRS to generate concrete results that have been praised by Sweden. In the agricultural sector, the project has facilitated the training of seed multipliers to boost the production of maize, soybeans, cowpeas, and cassava. Simultaneously, the local community network has been strengthened through the structuring and SMART training of 198 producer organizations, directly impacting 4,950 farmers, the majority of whom are women (2,910 women to 2,040 men), supported by 198 agricultural leaders. To respond adaptively and immediately to the heat waves experienced by the communities, a reforestation initiative, not included in the project's initial plan, was successfully implemented. The planting of over 240,000 fastgrowing trees has thus enabled the restoration of forest cover and optimized water retention directly in cultivated plots. The project has undergone a significant nutritional transformation. Driven by the momentum of Tudikolela, the CRS, and their partners, the Community-Based Nutrition (CBN) approach has been successfully implemented in 99 health centers. This innovative, multisectoral model unites agriculture, health, and education around a rigorous sevenstep program, supported by intensive training for health workers. On the ground, mobilization has scaled up considerably. The community network has grown significantly, from 99 to 402 liaison officers, which now allows for monthly monitoring and awarenessraising of each household. Dr. Danny, the project coordinator, explains, At first, families were hesitant to change their habits. But by coming every month, explaining the importance of exclusive breastfeeding, and showing how to enrich the diets of children and mothers with whole, locally sourced, four-star products, trust was established. Afterward, the mothers and young mothers eagerly awaited the liaison officers. The results of these efforts are concretely measured through a largescale screening campaign targeting nearly 21,000 vulnerable women and children. Thanks to these actions, the proportion of nutritionally healthy children under five has progressed encouragingly, climbing from 76% in 2022 to 80.5% in 2023. Dr. Danny, the project coordinator, summarizes the situation: The numbers are improving, and this proves that our multisectoral methodology is working. But we cannot declare victory. As long as global food insecurity persists and we lack readily available therapeutic treatments for severe cases, our fight will remain unfinished. We must scale up aid. Finally, the success of these interventions relies on strong integration within state institutions, the governorate, and technical services and ministries, particularly Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock, Rural Development, Health, Social Affairs, Planning, and Gender Equality. This close institutional collaboration has fostered a positive dynamic for improving local governance, while consolidating the project's lasting impact on food security and nutrition. In conclusion, the project has revitalized agriculture and strengthened peace through savings groups (SILC). It has transformed society by promoting gender equality and women's leadership, exceeding the objectives of SDG 5 through shared management of resources and households. The future of the project depends on sustaining these achievements after the donors' departure. Major challenges include a lack of infrastructure to evacuate the crops, the risk of overwork for women, and cultural resistance to this rapid social change
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
